Panchayat Libraries in Karnataka: Field Notes from Anekal

Field Immersion
Azim Premji Foundation, Bengaluru Urban, Karnataka
December 2024

Supervisor: Prof. Srishti Yadav (Azim Premji University, Bengaluru)

Fieldwork

I conducted 30 semi-structured informal interviews with key village stakeholders, including the Panchayat Development Officer, ward members, ASHA workers and Anganwadi workers, to understand government service delivery systems.

I independently designed the interview questionnaire and conducted an in-depth interview with the Panchayat librarian. The fieldwork provided a ground-level understanding of the functioning of Panchayat libraries and their role in the community, and informed a report on the establishment, administration, financial structure, monitoring, and current functioning of Panchayat libraries in Karnataka.

The fieldwork focused particularly on the Gram Panchayat Library at Neriga in Anekal taluk. The interview with the librarian provided information on library resources, procurement, financial constraints, administrative procedures, infrastructure, visitor records, educational demand, and the role of the library as a community space.

Report insights

Panchayat libraries and rural knowledge infrastructure

Gram Panchayat Libraries form an important part of rural knowledge infrastructure, providing access to reading materials, public information, and learning spaces. They play a role in education, community development, and access to information, particularly in rural areas where access to educational resources can be more limited.

The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the importance of these institutions. The closure of schools, colleges, and other educational institutions created additional barriers to educational resources for rural children. Children experienced disruptions in their learning routines and faced difficulties in accessing reading materials. During this period, libraries could provide an alternative source of educational materials and a space for students and other community members.

The fieldwork at Neriga indicated a clear decline in regular study routines during the period of closures, followed by a gradual return after reopening. Demand for examination-related materials increased after schools reopened, although procurement of new materials did not always keep pace with this demand.

Public library legislation in India

The development of public libraries in India has largely taken place through state-level legislation. Tamil Nadu was among the earliest states to enact public library legislation with the Tamil Nadu Public Libraries Act of 1948, which was implemented in 1950. Andhra Pradesh followed with the Public Libraries Act in 1960, while Karnataka enacted its library legislation in 1965.

Other states subsequently introduced public library legislation, including Maharashtra in 1967, West Bengal in 1979, Manipur, Haryana and Kerala in 1989, Mizoram and Goa in 1993, Odisha and Gujarat in 2001, Uttarakhand in 2005, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh in 2006, and Lakshadweep in 2007. Telangana’s public library legislation subsequently developed from the Andhra Pradesh Public Libraries Act following the reorganisation of Andhra Pradesh in 2014.

These legislative developments reflect the role of state governments in establishing public library systems and expanding access to information, education, and literacy.

The Karnataka Public Libraries Act, 1965

The Karnataka Public Libraries Act, 1965 provided the legal foundation for establishing and maintaining a comprehensive public library service across the state. The Act came into effect in 1966 and supported the development of libraries across different administrative levels, including state, district, taluk, and Gram Panchayat levels.

Karnataka became the third state in India to adopt a Library Act. The development of the state’s public library system was influenced by the work of Dr. S. R. Ranganathan, widely recognised as the Father of Library Science in India. The legislation provided the basis for expanding public library services across both rural and urban areas and aimed to promote equitable access to knowledge, education, and community development.

The Act also required rural libraries to maintain a copy of the Constitution of India. The public library system developed as a hierarchical structure extending from the state level through district and taluk levels to Gram Panchayat libraries.

In 1998, the Karnataka Public Libraries Act was amended to increase the annual grant for infrastructure development in district libraries from 3 percent to 6 percent of land revenue through the Karnataka Public Libraries (Amendment) Ordinance. The report also documents the extensive network of Gram Panchayat libraries that developed across the state.

Transfer to Rural Development and Panchayat Raj

In 2019, the management of rural libraries was transferred to the Department of Rural Development and Panchayat Raj (RDPR). Rural libraries were subsequently referred to as Gram Panchayat Library and Information Centres.

The transfer brought library management closer to the local governance system and placed Gram Panchayats in a more direct position in relation to the administration and management of rural libraries. The transition affected funding, monitoring, administrative oversight, procurement, inspections, and the role of librarians.

The post-2019 system also involved changes in administrative support, including regular salaries and inspections. At the local level, the fieldwork indicated that these changes were important in formalising administrative processes and providing greater institutional support to librarians.

The RDPR system also promoted initiatives intended to encourage reading and community participation, including Oduva Belaku, Pustaka Jolige, Odina Manege Hogona, Ammanigagi Ondu Pustaka, Chaduranga Adona, and Chinnara Chittara Abhiyana.

The fieldwork also indicated the presence of NGO-linked activities in Anekal through periodic reading events and limited infrastructure upgrades. However, day-to-day procurement of books and other resources remained constrained by local budgets and administrative processes.

Financial devolution

The report examines the role of library cess and other sources of funding in sustaining public libraries. Under the Karnataka Public Libraries Act, public libraries receive a share of property tax revenue collected by urban local bodies in the form of library cess. These resources are intended to support infrastructure, assets, books, subscriptions, and other library requirements.

Before the 2019 transition, the allocation and administration of these resources were primarily handled by the Department of Public Libraries. Following the transfer of rural libraries to RDPR, Gram Panchayats became more directly involved in managing library resources and local expenditure.

Public libraries are also supported through government grants, infrastructure and capacity-building resources, CSR contributions, donations, membership fees, revenue from services, local government allocations, and partnerships with educational institutions.

The fieldwork at Neriga showed how these financial constraints affect everyday library functioning. Recurring requirements such as books, basic furniture, and small repairs compete within limited local budgets. Requests for new materials can require repeated administrative follow-up, while the absence of a dedicated resource officer can create an additional bottleneck in procurement.

Monitoring and evaluation

Public libraries operate within a system of financial and administrative monitoring involving Gram Panchayats and RDPR. Libraries maintain records relating to visitors, expenditure, activities, and other aspects of their functioning. These records are submitted through the relevant Gram Panchayat and RDPR administrative channels.

The report also documents the role of inspections and audits in maintaining administrative and financial accountability. At the local level, the fieldwork at Neriga indicated that the librarian maintained visitor and expenditure registers and that records were reviewed through the Panchayat and RDPR system.

Annual audits and administrative oversight were part of the monitoring structure, while regular inspections and salary regularisation were identified as important post-2019 changes. These procedures influence the availability of resources, procurement processes, and the ability of libraries to respond to changing community needs.

The Neriga Gram Panchayat Library

The fieldwork at the Neriga Gram Panchayat Library in Anekal taluk provided a detailed view of the everyday functioning of a rural library.

The library housed approximately 11,000 books. However, a significant proportion of the collection consisted of older novels and textbooks. The librarian identified strong demand for updated educational resources, current textbooks, English storybooks, competitive examination guides, and multilingual content.

The gap between the existing collection and community demand was an important issue. The library possessed a substantial number of books, but the usefulness of the collection depended on whether the available materials remained relevant to the needs of current users.

The library also faced practical infrastructure constraints. Limited space and a shortage of study tables restricted the number of users that could be accommodated and affected the library’s ability to provide an effective study environment.

Community demand and educational resources

The fieldwork suggested that demand for library resources is closely connected to the educational needs of the surrounding community. Current textbooks, competitive examination guides, children’s books, and English-language materials were identified as important areas of demand.

The demand for examination-related materials was particularly relevant after the reopening of educational institutions. Students preparing for competitive examinations also required updated guides and study materials.

These observations point to the importance of regularly updating library collections rather than relying primarily on older books. The usefulness of a rural library therefore depends not only on the size of its collection but also on the relevance, currency, and accessibility of the materials available to users.

The fieldwork also highlighted the importance of basic physical infrastructure. Limited space and insufficient study tables constrained the ability of the library to function as a regular study and learning environment.

Community engagement

The report also considers the role of Panchayat libraries as community spaces rather than simply repositories of books.

The fieldwork highlighted possibilities for activities such as storytelling sessions, digital literacy programmes, personality development workshops, and cultural events. Such activities could increase regular participation and strengthen the library’s role as a shared community institution.

Community engagement can also help libraries respond to local educational and informational needs. Activities aimed at children, students, and young people preparing for examinations could provide additional reasons for regular library use.

The fieldwork suggested that rebuilding regular footfall requires attention not only to books and infrastructure but also to the activities and services that make the library relevant to the surrounding community.

Key field observation

The field immersion connected the formal institutional structure of Panchayat libraries with their day-to-day functioning at the local level.

The experience showed how funding, procurement, infrastructure, educational demand, administrative procedures, and community participation interact in shaping the functioning of a rural library.

The Neriga fieldwork also illustrated the difference between having a formal institutional structure and having the resources required for that structure to function effectively. The library had a substantial collection and an established administrative system, but continued to face constraints related to updated materials, procurement, space, furniture, and community engagement.

The fieldwork therefore provided a practical perspective on the functioning and community role of Panchayat libraries within Karnataka’s broader public library system. It also highlighted the importance of linking administrative reforms and financial devolution with the everyday needs of librarians and library users.
